INDIO, California (CNN) -- For some concertgoers, the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival really kicked into action on Day Two. Festival attendees enjoy the music Saturday, Day Two of the Coachella music festival in Indio, California. Day One was leisurely and pleasant -- the weather was mild, the acts were fairly mellow and the big headliner was Paul McCartney. On Day Two, someone took the dial and turned it up a notch, as the desert sun beat down a little harder, the music pumped a little louder and the crowds who packed the VIP tent threw a little more attitude. There were the usual celebrity sightings. Jake Gyllenhaal and Reese Witherspoon snuck in the back just as rapper M.I.A. hit the stage, Paris Hilton took in Travis Barker and DJ AM's set in the Sahara tent and David Hasselhoff was spotted making out with a mystery lady near the restrooms. Forty-six acts performed on five stages scattered about the grassy field of the Empire Polo Club near Palm Springs, California. Massive eco-friendly art installations fashioned from scrap metal and reclaimed wood doubled as shelter from the heat, as well as mini-stages for dancers and performance artists. There was good buzz for thenewno2, an indie-pop band fronted by Oli Hecks and Dhani Harrison, whose vocals are reminiscent of his late father, George, but warmer, and less haunting. "It's the first festival we've ever played, and our 12th gig overall," said Harrison. "Normally with festivals, people come to check you out, stand in the back, and then move on pretty quickly, even if they like you -- but people stayed! It's the best performance we've ever had." Unfortunately Fleet Foxes was not so lucky. The Seattle,Washington, group's delicate baroque harmonies were drowned out by the world music beats of Thievery Corporation's percussion section bleeding over from the neighboring main stage, as one of their female vocalists crowd-surfed. As usual, the day's line-up was a mix of up-and-coming indie artists sprinkled with tried-and-true veteran acts. The Killers have played Coachella in both capacities. The Las Vegas, Nevada, quartet received their first invitation from festival organizers in 2004, the same year their debut album, "Hot Fuss," was released. "We played at 11:30 a.m. in a tent. It was 150 degrees out, and backstage, it smelled like horse droppings," said drummer Ronnie Vannucci, referencing the fact that there are certain consequences to holding an event on a polo field in the desert. This time, as the marquee act, The Killers enjoyed their own backstage compound decked out with a white picket fence, tablecloths and festive party lights in the shape of daisies. Palm trees gently swayed in the distance, silhouetted against the desert backdrop. You could hear the crowd going crazy for a feisty M.I.A. slotted on the main stage before The Killers. Vannucci and his three bandmates had just rolled in on their tour bus from Vegas. He spoke with CNN while warming up his hands and wrists with drumming exercises. "With festivals, you have to realize the audience is not necessarily there to see YOU. So we'll play some stuff off our new album, 'Day and Age,' and work in some songs that everybody knows, like 'Mr. Brightside' from our first album." Half an hour later, The Killers took the stage, opening their set with their latest hit, "Human." Frontman Brandon Flowers soon had the crowd singing the along to the perplexing lyrics, "Are we human, or are we dancer?" At Coachella, it doesn't matter if you're human or if you're dancer. But if you're dancer, you'll probably be relegated to one of the mini-stages inside an art installation. "The first time I heard about Coachella 10 years ago, I thought, 'That could be the cool festival here in America," said Vannucci. "It's since become a successful festival with good bands, swarms of people coming in from all over the world -- even art elements. It's strange to think we're headlining one night."

**INDIO, California (CNN)** — For many concertgoers, the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival truly hit its stride on Day Two. While the festival’s opening day was a relaxed and pleasant affair—characterized by temperate weather, mellow acts, and a headlining performance by Paul McCartney—Saturday saw the event dial up its intensity. As the desert sun beat down with greater fervor, the music reverberated louder, and the crowds packing the VIP tent exuded an elevated swagger. 

Celebrity sightings were plentiful. Jake Gyllenhaal and Reese Witherspoon quietly slipped in through the back just as rapper M.I.A. took the stage; Paris Hilton took in Travis Barker and DJ AM’s set in the Sahara tent; and David Hasselhoff was spotted kissing an unidentified companion near the restrooms.

A total of 46 acts performed across five stages distributed throughout the grassy grounds of the Empire Polo Club near Palm Springs. Towering, eco-friendly art installations constructed from scrap metal and reclaimed wood served a dual purpose: providing shade from the scorching heat and acting as elevated platforms for dancers and performance artists. 

Generating considerable buzz was thenewno2, an indie-pop group fronted by Oli Hecks and Dhani Harrison. The vocal delivery of the younger Harrison evokes that of his late father, George, though with a warmer, less haunting timbre. 

"It's the first festival we've ever played, and our 12th gig overall," Harrison remarked. "Normally with festivals, people come to check you out, stand in the back, and then move on pretty quickly, even if they like you—but people stayed! It's the best performance we've ever had."

Regrettably, Fleet Foxes were not as fortunate. The Seattle-based group’s delicate baroque harmonies were largely overwhelmed by the sound bleed from the neighboring main stage, where Thievery Corporation’s heavy world-music percussion thundered as one of their female vocalists crowd-surfed.

As is customary for Coachella, the day’s lineup offered a balanced mix of emerging indie talent and seasoned veteran acts. The Killers have experienced the festival from both sides of that spectrum. The Las Vegas quartet received their first invitation from festival organizers in 2004, the same year they released their debut album, *Hot Fuss*. 

"We played at 11:30 a.m. in a tent. It was 150 degrees out, and backstage, it smelled like horse droppings," said drummer Ronnie Vannucci, offering a candid reminder of the realities associated with hosting a festival on an active desert polo field.

This time, as the marquee act, The Killers enjoyed an exclusive backstage compound adorned with a white picket fence, dressed tables, and festive daisy-shaped string lights. In the distance, palm trees swayed gently against the silhouette of the desert backdrop, while the thunderous cheers of the crowd echoed from the main stage, where a spirited M.I.A. performed directly before them. 

Having just arrived on their tour bus from Las Vegas, Vannucci and his three bandmates prepared for their set. "So we'll play some stuff off our new album, *Day & Age*, and work in some songs that everybody knows, like 'Mr. Brightside' from our first album."

Half an hour later, The Killers took the stage, opening with their latest hit, "Human." Frontman Brandon Flowers soon had the audience singing along to the famously perplexing line, *"Are we human, or are we dancer?"* At Coachella, the distinction hardly matters—though anyone identifying as a dancer would likely be relegated to one of the mini-stages inside the art installations.

"The first time I heard about Coachella 10 years ago, I thought, 'That could be the cool festival here in America,'" Vannucci reflected. "It's since become a successful festival with good bands, swarms of people coming in from all over the world—even art elements. It's strange to think we're headlining one night."

**INDIO, Calif. (CNN) —** If Friday at the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival was about finding the groove, Saturday was about blowing the roof off the desert. 

Day 2 of the annual double-weekend extravaganza in Indio, California, saw a palpable surge in energy across the Empire Polo Club grounds. Powered by cooler evening temperatures, a star-studded audience, and a triumphant, hit-heavy headlining set from rock royalty **The Killers**, the festival reached a fever pitch.

From the moment gates opened, festivalgoers seemed to have shaken off the first-day fatigue. The Sahara Tent was packed early with high-octane electronic sets, while the Outdoor Theatre saw thousands kicking up dust during sunset performances. But as night fell, all roads led to the Coachella Main Stage for the night’s most anticipated moment.

### The Killers Bring Las Vegas Glam and Anthem Rock

Taking the main stage just after 11:00 p.m., Las Vegas alt-rock titans The Killers delivered a masterclass in festival headlining. 

Frontman Brandon Flowers—dapper as ever in a tailored, shimmering blazer—commanded the stage with unmatched charisma from the first note of "Somebody Told Me."

"We’ve been coming to the desert for a long time, but there’s nothing quite like this," Flowers told the roaring crowd of over 100,000 fans. "We came to bring you some joy tonight!"

And joy they delivered. The band's 90-minute set was an unrelenting parade of mid-2000s classics and modern hits, including "Human," "When You Were Young," and "All These Things That I've Done"—the latter prompting a massive, field-wide singalong of its iconic "I've got soul, but I'm not a soldier" refrain. 

The climax came with a explosive, confetti-filled rendition of "Mr. Brightside," a track that effectively turned the entire polo field into a giant, pulsating dance floor. 

"They proved why they are stadium legends," said Marcus Vance, 29, who traveled from Chicago for the festival. "Day 1 was fun, but The Killers just set a completely different bar for the weekend. The energy was electric."

### A-List Sightings and VIP Buzz

Coachella is as much a fashion runway and celebrity hub as it is a music event, and Saturday did not disappoint on the star-power front. 

The VIP Rose Garden and exclusive backstage lounges were bustling with Hollywood elite and pop culture icons. Spotted taking in the sights—and dodging phone cameras—were Hailey and Justin Bieber, Timothée Chalamet, and supermodel Kendall Jenner. Actor Pedro Pascal was also seen grooving near the sound booth during an late-afternoon indie set, much to the delight of nearby fans.

Fashion on Day 2 shifted toward high-energy, futuristic streetwear and Y2K revivals, with silver metallic accents, oversized leather jackets, and sheer layering dominating the crowd. 

### High Energy Across the Grounds

The Killers weren't the only ones driving Saturday's momentum. Earlier in the evening, the undercard delivered standout moments that kept the crowd's energy soaring. 

Over at the Mojave tent, a surprise guest appearance by pop sensation Dua Lipa during a DJ set sent social media into a frenzy, while the festival’s iconic giant Ferris wheel sparkled against a backdrop of glowing neon art installations and laser shows.

Security and medical personnel reported a smooth night despite the larger, more active crowds, noting that the shift to cooler night temperatures helped keep festivalgoers in high spirits.

As the music faded around 1:00 a.m. and fans began the long trek back to the campgrounds and shuttle lines, the consensus was clear: Day 2 brought the heat, the hits, and the Hollywood glamour. 

All eyes now turn to Day 3, where the festival will wrap up its first weekend with another stacked lineup—though Saturday night’s high-octane spectacle will be a tough act to follow.

**INDIO, Calif.** — If Friday at the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival was defined by emotional reverie and classic rock royalty, Saturday belonged entirely to the vibrant, restless spirit of contemporary indie, dance, and rock. 

Following Sir Paul McCartney’s legendary, tear-jerking opening-night performance, the atmosphere on Day 2 at the Empire Polo Club shifted dramatically. The reverent hush gave way to an electric, party-fueled urgency. Temperatures soared past 90 degrees during the day, forcing thousands of sun-baked festival-goers into brief pockets of shade before cooler evening breezes swept over the Palm Springs desert, bringing out a wilder, higher-energy night crowd.

Towering over the sprawling green fields were this year's signature large-scale art installations. Attendees congregated around the glowing *Spire*, a massive light-emitting structure, and marvelled at towering kinetic metal sculptures that pulsed with fire and light as darkness fell. The iconic giant origami cranes and solar-powered interactive installations provided a surreal, playground-like backdrop for the day's musical marathon.

The festival’s expanding cultural footprint was also reflected in the star-studded VIP enclosures. Celebrity sightings were frequent throughout the day, with Paris Hilton, Drew Barrymore, Justin Long, Kate Bosworth, Alexander Skarsgård, and *Gossip Girl* stars Penn Badgley and Blake Lively spotted navigating the rose gardens and weaving through the main crowd.

Musically, Day 2 delivered a seamless cross-genre blend, starting in the afternoon with an intricate performance by Thenewno2 on the Mojave Stage. Led by Dhani Harrison—son of the late Beatle George Harrison—the band offered a sophisticated blend of alternative rock and subtle electronica.

"Playing out here in the middle of the desert with all this incredible energy—it's wild," Dhani Harrison remarked backstage following his set. "You can feel the history and the love people have for the music out here. Following my dad's old mate Paul’s set last night... it’s a total trip, but it feels right."

As the sun began to dip behind the San Jacinto Mountains, Seattle indie-folk outfit Fleet Foxes captivated a massive gathering at the Outdoor Theatre. The twilight setting proved to be the ideal backdrop for their lush, pastoral harmonies. Tracks like "White Winter Hymnal" and "Mykonos" echoed across the grass, prompting quiet awe and sweeping sing-alongs from a crowd blanketed in purple and orange sunset light.

The tranquil mood was promptly shattered later in the evening when rap-rave powerhouse M.I.A. took the stage. Performing just two months after giving birth, the artist delivered a fierce, unapologetic, high-octane set that sent shockwaves through the field. Surrounded by neon visuals and frantic strobe lights, she whipped the audience into a frenzy with tracks like "Boyz" and her global smash "Paper Planes," which had tens of thousands pumping their fists and mimicking gunshot sound effects in unison.

The night culminated on the Main Stage with headliners The Killers. Taking the stage in a suit adorned with his signature feathered epaulets, frontman Brandon Flowers led the Las Vegas quartet through a polished, stadium-sized set of desert-hued synth-pop and anthemic rock. Opening with "Human" and powering through hits like "Somebody Told Me," "Smile Like You Mean It," and "Mr. Brightside," the band proved they were more than capable of commanding Coachella’s peak Saturday night slot.

The band was well aware of the monumental task of headlining the night after a Beatle. 

"Following Sir Paul is a bit terrifying, to be honest," confessed Killers drummer Ronnie Vannucci after the show. "You're stepping onto a stage that was literally vibrating with rock history 24 hours ago. But we’re a desert band. Coming out here to Indio feels like playing in our backyard, just with 60,000 of our closest friends."

As Day 2 drew to a close with a massive fireworks display over The Killers' triumphant encore of "When You Were Young," dusty concertgoers dispersed into the night—weary, sun-burnt, but primed for Sunday’s final stretch.

**INDIO, Calif.** — If Friday night at the Empire Polo Club was a gentle, collective sigh of nostalgia led by Sir Paul McCartney’s acoustic-tinged, sing-along heavy headline set, Saturday was a guttural, 100-decibel roar. 

By 3:00 PM on Day Two, any lingering warmth from McCartney’s breezy, multi-generational sunset reverie had evaporated into the 95-degree desert heat. In its place was a visceral, sweat-soaked energy driven by a Saturday lineup determined to test the structural integrity of the festival’s subwoofers. Where Friday felt like a communal picnic, Saturday was a marathon in dusty boots.

The tonal shift was immediate. Early afternoon crowds bypassed the shaded lawns to swarm the Sahara Tent, where relentless 140-BPM 808s kicked up plumes of dust that hung like smoke under the desert sun. Over on the Outdoor Theatre, aggressive synth-driven rock replaced the campfire melodies of the night before, trading sweeping harmonies for walls of feedback and mosh pits that churned up the dry grass.

However, Saturday’s sheer volume brought with it the festival’s most glaring issue of the weekend: severe sound bleed. 

As the layout of the Polo Grounds expanded to accommodate record crowds, the sonic boundaries between stages disintegrated under the weight of Saturday’s louder performers. Over at the Mojave Tent, a rising indie singer-songwriter’s delicate, intimate balladry was repeatedly hijacked by the monstrous, low-end rumble bleeding over from the nearby Sahara Tent. During a quiet acoustic bridge, the crowd didn’t hear delicate fingerpicking; they felt the tactile vibration of a dubstep drop happening 200 yards away.

Backstage in the artist compound, the sonic crossfire was a primary topic of conversation among performers cooling off in the air-conditioned trailers.

"I was in the middle of our quietest, most emotional track—a song I wrote about my late grandfather—and suddenly the entire stage started physically shaking from a trap beat next door," laughed Maya Lin, lead vocalist of the dream-pop outfit *Glass Horizon*, dabbing sweat from her forehead. "You just have to pivot. I literally shouted into the mic, 'Alright, guess we’re dancing to both!' You can't fight the bass out here. You just survive it."

Other performers leaned into the chaos. British electronic producer DJ Kael, fresh off a thunderous, pyrotechnic-heavy set at the Gobi Tent, offered a different perspective on the day's high-stakes noise war. 

"Look, Paul McCartney was magic yesterday—a total legend, super classy, soft lighting," Kael said, clutching an iced matcha behind the main stage. "But Friday was for the parents. Saturday is for the sinners. My job today wasn't to make you weep about 'Hey Jude.' My job was to blow the dust out of your lungs and make sure your ears are ringing until Tuesday. If we’re bleeding into other stages, that just means we’re winning the decibel race."

By the time night fell, turning the festival grounds into a glowing expanse of neon palm trees and towering art installations, the energy had reached a fever pitch. A massive, dense crowd flooded the Main Stage for a head-spinning, high-production hip-hop set that featured unexpected guest appearances, blinding laser arrays, and fireworks that rattled the teeth of everyone within a half-mile radius.

Where Day One offered reverence and quiet magic, Day Two offered adrenaline, overstimulation, and a stark reminder that Coachella is, at its core, an endurance test. As thousands of dust-covered festivalgoers trudged toward the shuttles after midnight—ears buzzing and voices hoarse—the calm of Sir Paul felt a universe away. 

Sunday lies ahead, but Saturday proved that when the desert turns up the volume, there is no turning back.
